strengths: Compelling and timely core motivation: Bridging the gap between the sample efficiency/low variance of pathwise policy gradients and the low memory overhead/simplicity of on-policy RL without relying on large off-policy replay buffers is a significant practical problem.

Well-motivated algorithm design: Combining on-policy TD(\lambda) targets, maximum entropy exploration, dual-adapted KL regularization, and modern architectural stabilizers (HL-Gauss categorical loss, layer normalization) yields a cohesive and principled framework.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The paper conducts rigorous benchmarks across 23 continuous control tasks in MuJoCo Playground DMC, 8 manipulation tasks in ManiSkill, and 10 discrete tasks in Atari. The use of robust statistical aggregation metrics (IQM, median, bootstrapped CIs) and reliability metrics (Chan et al., 2020) provides convincing evidence.

Thorough ablations: The ablations clearly isolate the contributions of the pathwise estimator, the KL penalty, the HL-Gauss regression loss, and buffer size scaling, which validates the design choices.
Generalizes across action spaces: Showing that the algorithm extends naturally to discrete action spaces via closed-form expectations (D-REPPO) adds breadth and practical value.
weaknesses: Incremental algorithmic novelty: Most individual components (TD(\lambda), entropy and KL dual updates, HL-Gauss regression, self-predictive auxiliary representations) are established techniques from prior literature. While their synthesis and demonstration in an on-policy pathwise framework is valuable, the conceptual novelty is moderate.

Mixed utility of auxiliary representation loss: The ablation study reveals that the latent self-prediction loss has inconsistent benefits across tasks (and occasionally degrades performance), yet it remains part of the default algorithm specification. A clearer heuristic or criteria for when to enable/disable it would be beneficial.

Minor presentation polish and typesetting issues: There are several broken references and typos in the manuscript, e.g., 'loss formulation in ??' on page 7, 'perforamnce above the PPO baseline with these appraoches' on page 9, and the incomplete sentence 'Our code is available a' on page 2.

strengths: Compelling conceptual premise: bridging the gap between low-variance pathwise policy gradients (traditionally confined to off-policy methods with large replay buffers) and the simplicity, sample reuse, and low memory footprint of on-policy actor-critic frameworks.

Comprehensive and rigorous empirical evaluation: evaluated across 23 continuous control tasks from the MuJoCo Playground DMC suite and 8 robotic manipulation tasks from ManiSkill 3, with 20 seeds and appropriate statistical aggregate metrics (mean, median, IQM, and reliability metrics).

Thorough ablation studies that effectively isolate the contributions of pathwise gradients, categorical HL-Gauss loss, dual-parameter KL/entropy regularization, layer normalization, and buffer size scaling.

Competitive performance and practical utility: matches or exceeds FastTD3 while requiring orders of magnitude less memory (eliminating the multi-gigabyte off-policy replay buffer), and significantly outperforms standard on-policy baselines like PPO in sample efficiency, stability, and final return.
Includes a well-thought-out extension to discrete control tasks (D-REPPO) evaluated on Atari-10, demonstrating the generality of the formulation.
weaknesses: Several components (HL-Gauss categorical regression, TD-lambda targets, dual Lagrangian adaptation for entropy/KL, and self-predictive representations) are drawn directly from recent literature; the primary novelty is the synthesis and adaptation of these components into a unified on-policy pathwise framework.

Baseline comparability: It is not entirely clear whether the PPO baselines incorporate the same architectural improvements (e.g., LayerNorm, categorical value loss, or auxiliary self-prediction) that are provided to REPPO, making it somewhat difficult to decouple algorithmic improvements from representation learning advancements.

Minor formatting and text errors: broken reference on page 7 ('We present the mathematical form of the loss formulation in ??'), truncated sentence at the bottom of page 2 ('Our code is available a'), and typographical errors in Section 4.2 ('perforamnce', 'appraoches').

In Equation 15, when the KL constraint is violated, the objective completely drops the value and entropy terms, optimizing solely for KL minimization; more justification on the numerical behavior and stability of this hard switching mechanism compared to standard Lagrangian relaxation or clipped surrogates would strengthen the paper.

strengths: Compelling motivation: Addresses a key bottleneck in massively parallel GPU-based reinforcement learning by combining the low variance of pathwise policy gradients with the low memory footprint and stability of purely on-policy data collection.

Well-executed algorithmic synthesis: The combination of multi-step TD(lambda) targets, categorical value learning via HL-Gauss, and dual automatic tuning of both entropy and KL-divergence constraints effectively mitigates the common pitfalls of value-based policy learning.

Thorough empirical evaluation: The paper evaluates across 23 MuJoCo Playground tasks and 8 ManiSkill manipulation tasks with 20 seeds, reporting robust aggregate metrics (IQM, median, mean with 95% CIs) and reliability metrics.

Comprehensive ablations: The authors systematically analyze each component (pathwise vs. score-based, KL constraint, HL-Gauss loss, LayerNorm, and auxiliary representation loss) across multiple data scales.
weaknesses: Incremental conceptual novelty: Most of the individual ingredients—HL-Gauss categorical loss, dual Lagrangian entropy/KL tuning, layer normalization, self-predictive auxiliary representations, and multi-step on-policy targets—are adopted directly from existing literature (e.g., SAC, REPS, Farebrother et al., Gallici et al.), making the work primarily an empirical recipe and engineering integration.

Heuristic nature of the policy objective switch: Equation 15 relies on an ad-hoc hard switch/clipping mechanism when the sample KL exceeds the target threshold, rather than a standard primal-dual optimization or exact penalty method; theoretical justification for convergence under this switched loss is lacking.

Inconsistent utility of auxiliary tasks: The latent self-prediction loss exhibits mixed effects—aiding learning in sparse reward settings while hurting performance in others—yet it remains part of the default baseline specification without an adaptive gating mechanism.

Drafting and presentation oversights: The manuscript contains multiple unfinished text fragments and unresolved references, such as an incomplete sentence at the bottom of page 2 ('Our code is available a'), a broken reference on page 7 ('loss formulation in ??'), and several typographical errors (e.g., 'appraoches', 'perforamnce' on page 9).

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: enabling stable and sample-efficient pathwise policy gradients in an on-policy, massively parallel simulation (MPS) setting without the large memory overhead of replay buffers.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 31 continuous control tasks (23 MuJoCo Playground DMC tasks and 8 ManiSkill3 environments) following rigorous statistical evaluation protocols (IQM, median, mean with bootstrapped CIs).
Thorough ablation study analyzing key design components (HL-Gauss categorical regression, dual-variable KL regularization, layer normalization, auxiliary self-prediction, and batch sizes).
Strong practical relevance: achieves competitive performance with off-policy methods (e.g., FastTD3) while maintaining a drastically smaller memory footprint and comparable wall-clock speed to PPO.
weaknesses: Many algorithmic components are combinations of existing techniques (HL-Gauss from Farebrother et al., self-prediction auxiliary tasks, dual Lagrangian updates reminiscent of SAC/MPO), making the algorithmic novelty somewhat incremental.

Several presentation bugs and typos that require proofreading: e.g., on page 10 there is a broken reference ('reported in ??'), Algorithm 1 contains an unmatched bracket in the auxiliary loss line, and Equation 19 contains an evident copy-paste error where the update for $\beta$ uses the entropy objective $(H[\pi_\theta(x)] - H_{\text{target}})$ instead of the KL divergence.

The auxiliary latent prediction task shows mixed effectiveness across domains (improving some but degrading others), yet the paper offers limited guidance on when to enable or disable it beyond empirical trial-and-error.

strengths: Compelling and timely motivation: bringing the sample efficiency and low-variance gradient benefits of pathwise (reparameterized / DPG) policy gradients into the purely on-policy, massively parallel simulation (MPS) regime where PPO typically dominates.

Well-designed algorithmic framework: the combination of maximum entropy TD(\lambda) targets, forward KL trust-region constraints with dual adaptive multiplier tuning, and categorical value loss (HL-Gauss) provides a coherent recipe that effectively resolves value divergence without requiring large replay buffers.

Strong and rigorous empirical evaluation: experiments span 23 tasks from MuJoCo Playground DMC and 8 manipulation tasks from ManiSkill3, utilizing aggregate metrics (IQM, median, bootstrapped CIs) adhering to modern RL evaluation standards.

Effective baseline comparisons and ablations: the paper compares against both Brax and heavily tuned PPO, as well as the off-policy FastTD3 (evaluating both large and small memory regimes). The ablations clearly isolate the contributions of the KL constraint, HL-Gauss loss, LayerNorm, and the auxiliary objective.
weaknesses: Several presentation and mathematical typos in key equations: Equation (19) contains a copy-paste error where the dual update for \beta uses the entropy difference $(H[\pi_\theta(x)] - H_{\text{target}})$ instead of the KL divergence $(D_{\text{KL}} - KL_{\text{target}})$; Section 4.1 contains an unresolved LaTeX reference ('in ??'); and the strikethrough formatting in Section 3.1.1 is messy.

Incremental conceptual novelty: the method primarily synthesizes existing techniques—combining continuous-action pathwise gradients with on-policy TD(\lambda) (extending PQN), dual Lagrangian updates for KL and entropy (similar to REPS, MPO, and Nauman & Cygan, 2025), HL-Gauss regression (Farebrother et al., 2024), and self-predictive representations (Schwarzer et al., 2021).

Inconsistent utility of the auxiliary loss: as the authors note, the self-predictive auxiliary task has mixed performance across tasks (improving some while degrading others), making its inclusion in the default algorithmic recipe questionable without clear selection heuristics.

Scope limited to state-based continuous control: the evaluation is restricted to low-dimensional state observations in GPU simulators; testing whether the stability of on-policy pathwise updates transfers to visual observations or other settings where on-policy RL is standard would strengthen the paper's generality.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: bridging the gap between high-variance score-function policy gradients (e.g., PPO) and memory-heavy off-policy pathwise methods (e.g., SAC, FastTD3) in massively parallel simulation environments.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 31 continuous control environments (23 MuJoCo Playground DMC tasks and 8 ManiSkill3 tasks) using rigorous statistical aggregation metrics (IQM, median, bootstrapped confidence intervals).

Detailed ablation study isolating the contributions of key components (KL regularization, HL-Gauss categorical loss, layer normalization, auxiliary representation learning) under different batch/buffer sizes.
Strong practical results: achieves performance on par with large-buffer off-policy methods (FastTD3) while using a fraction of the memory footprint and maintaining comparable wall-clock speed to PPO.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the method primarily combines existing components (TD(\lambda) on Q-functions, maximum entropy RL, dual-variable trust-region tuning from REPS/MPO, HL-Gauss loss from Farebrother et al., and latent self-prediction auxiliary objectives) rather than introducing a fundamentally new theoretical or algorithmic paradigm.

Several noticeable drafting errors and missing references: Equation (19) contains a copy-paste error where it minimizes the entropy difference instead of the KL divergence constraint $(D_{KL} - KL_{\text{target}})$; Section 4.1 contains an unresolved reference '??'; and the code URL placeholder in Section 1 is left blank.

Inconsistent notation in value target definitions: Equations (12) and (13) mix trajectory time indices $t$ and lookahead steps $n$, making the exact rollout structure slightly ambiguous without checking Algorithm 1.

The auxiliary latent self-prediction loss exhibits mixed empirical benefits across tasks (acknowledged by the authors), suggesting that the unified recipe is not yet entirely cohesive across all problem domains.
